evals.name: hashing-is-not-an-expect
evals.prompt: The two-build server at {fixture} needs password hashing for sign-up and sign-in. I know jBCrypt on the JVM, so my plan is `expect fun hashPassword` / `expect fun verifyPassword` in server-common, jBCrypt in the JVM actual and something else in the native actual. Set it up — the build changes and where each file goes — and tell me if you would do it differently. Do not build; there is no Gradle wrapper.
evals.expected_output: No expect/actual pair: one implementation in commonMain on a multiplatform library whose linuxX64 artefact was checked, with the reason that two actuals diverge silently — a hash made by one build refused by the other shows up on the day the image is switched.
expectations: The answer does not add an expect/actual pair for hashing; the implementation is one function in server-common's commonMain

The reason is given: the compiler checks an expect/actual pair for signature and never for behaviour, so two hashing implementations can produce hashes the other build refuses, and nothing fails until deployment
The library chosen is multiplatform, and the answer says it checked (or that one must check) that it publishes a linuxX64 artefact before depending on it from commonMain
No JVM-only coordinate (jBCrypt, or any `-jvm` artefact) is added to commonMain
If the library needs a provider or engine per platform, it is declared in each build module (server and server-native), not left to arrive transitively
A test for hashing and verification is placed in server-common's commonTest so that it runs on both targets
readEnv is left as the only expect, or the answer says the count of pairs stays at one

evals.name: a-blocking-handler-decides-the-engine
evals.prompt: The service at {fixture} has a bad p99 under load. A colleague read that Netty costs half the CPU per request of CIO and wants to switch the engine. Should we? If yes, make the change; if not, say what to change instead. Either way give the reasoning a reviewer can check. Do not build; there is no Gradle wrapper.
evals.expected_output: The handlers block a thread, which is the case where the engine comparison flips: Netty's call group defaults to the processor count (two here) and would be the worst default; the options are to keep CIO, or to take Netty with callGroupSize raised, or to move the blocking off the handler — and to measure.
expectations: The answer notices that every handler blocks a thread on JDBC, and says the 'Netty is cheaper' result holds for handlers that never block
It states that Netty's callGroupSize defaults to the processor count — two on this pod — so blocking handlers would queue behind two threads
It does not simply swap CIO for Netty with default settings

If Netty is chosen, callGroupSize is raised explicitly with a number tied to the pool size or the blocking time; if CIO is kept, the answer says its IO workers are the slack that keeps blocking handlers serving
Moving the JDBC call off the handler's thread (withContext(Dispatchers.IO) in a repository) is offered as the change that makes the engine question separate from the blocking one
The answer recommends measuring on this service before and after rather than quoting the per-request numbers as this service's
The engine stays a decision of the build's entry point; nothing about it is pushed into shared code
